WASHINGTON (CNN) -- A member of the royal family of Abu Dhabi who was captured on videotape torturing an Afghan grain dealer has reportedly been detained, a senior U.S. State Department official told CNN Saturday. Sheikh Issa bin Zayed al Nahyan, pictured here, allegedly tortured a business associate on videotape. The official said the government of the United Arab Emirates, which includes Abu Dhabi as one of its seven emirates, told the State Department that Sheikh Issa bin Zayed al Nahyan is under house arrest pending an investigation, but that the United States has not independently confirmed the development. The videotape emerged last month in a federal civil lawsuit filed in Houston, Texas, by Bassam Nabulsi, a U.S. citizen, against the sheikh. Former business partners, the men had a falling out, in part over the tape. In a statement to CNN, the sheikh's U.S. attorney said Nabulsi is using the videotape to influence the court over a business dispute. The tape of the heinous torture session is delaying the ratification of a civil nuclear deal between the United Arab Emirates and the United States, senior U.S. officials familiar with the case have said. The senior U.S. officials said the administration has held off on the ratification process because it believes sensitivities over the story can hurt its passage. On Saturday, Human Rights Watch called the sheikh's reported detention "a significant development" but said the UAE government needs to do more to restore confidence in its judicial system. "The videotape of this episode shocked the world," said Sarah Leah Whitson, Middle East director at Human Rights Watch. "The report of the arrest was reassuring, but now the government needs to make the details public. Secretive prosecutions will not deter further abuses and torture." On the tape, Sheikh Issa appears to burn with rage. Apparently believing he was cheated in a business deal, the sheikh was trying to extract a confession from the Afghan grain dealer. With a private security officer assisting, Sheikh Issa is seen stuffing sand in the Afghan's mouth. As the grain dealer pleads and whimpers, he is beaten with a nailed board, burned in the genitals with a cigarette lighter, shocked with a cattle prod and led to believe he would be shot. Salt is literally poured on his wounds. The 45 minutes of torture appears on a nearly three-hour-long videotape shot in late 2004 in the desert outside Abu Dhabi. It was made at the direction of the sheikh himself. The tape has been viewed by CNN.  Watch portions of the tape and Nabulsi tell his story » . After international concerns over the tape mounted in late April, Abu Dhabi's government issued a statement saying it deplored the contents of the video and planned an immediate and comprehensive review of it. The sheikh, who holds no official government position, is the half-brother of the UAE's ruler, President Sheikh Khalifa bin Zayed Al Nahyan. Human Rights Watch sent a April 28 letter to the president imploring him to form "an independent body" to probe both the torture and and the "failure" of the UAE's Interior Ministry "to bring those involved to justice." The group reiterated that call Saturday. As for the grain dealer, UAE officials say he survived the ordeal, and said the sheikh and the grain dealer settled the matter privately by agreeing not to bring formal charges against each other. However, Nabulsi's attorney, Anthony Buzbee, said the grain dealer can't be located and it is not known whether he is alive.

**Royal Scandal in Abu Dhabi: Torture Video Triggers House Arrest and Derails US-UAE Nuclear Deal**

The United Arab Emirates’ carefully curated image as a modern, stable, and law-abiding hub of international commerce has been severely shaken following the release of a shocking video depicting systemic torture carried out by a senior member of the Abu Dhabi royal family. The footage, which shows Sheikh Issa bin Zayed al Nahyan savagely abusing an Afghan grain merchant over a minor financial disagreement, has ignited international outrage, forced the UAE government into unprecedented damage-control measures, and thrown a major bilateral agreement with the United States into jeopardy.

### The Incident and the Tape

The controversy centers on a leaked 45-minute videotape showing Sheikh Issa—a brother of the UAE’s effective ruler at the time, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Zayed al Nahyan—inflicting horrific physical violence on Mohammed Shah Poor, an Afghan merchant. The dispute reportedly stemmed from a commercial disagreement involving missing grain valued at roughly $5,000. 

In the footage, which was smuggled out of the country by a former business associate and broadcast internationally by ABC News, Sheikh Issa is seen pouring salt into the merchant’s open wounds, beating him with wooden planks studded with nails, lighting his genitals on fire, and using an SUV to run over the immobilized victim. A man wearing a UAE police uniform is also visible participating in the assault, raising grave questions about state complicity in the royal's actions.

### Official Response and House Arrest

The immediate broadcast of the video triggered an avalanche of international condemnation. Initially, the UAE Ministry of Interior dismissed the incident, declaring that the matter had been settled privately between the parties involved. However, as global pressure intensified, the UAE government altered its stance to protect its international reputation. 

In an unprecedented move against a member of the ruling family, UAE authorities announced that Sheikh Issa had been placed under house arrest pending an official criminal investigation by the Ministry of Justice. Government officials publicly insisted that the country’s judicial framework applies to all citizens equally, maintaining that "no individual is above the law."

### Demands for Transparency and Human Rights Reform

Despite the government's public assurances, international human rights organizations remain skeptical. Advocacy groups, including Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International, have openly questioned whether the house arrest is merely a public relations gesture meant to defuse international media attention.

Human rights advocates are demanding a fully transparent, independent prosecution, open to public and international oversight. They argue that the case serves as a crucial litmus test for the UAE judicial system, which has long been criticized for protecting powerful elites from legal consequences. Rights groups emphasize that establishing true credibility will require not only the prosecution of Sheikh Issa, but also a thorough investigation into the security personnel who assisted in the assault, alongside systemic reforms to prevent police officers from acting as private enforcers for the monarchy.

### Geopolitical Fallout: The US-UAE Nuclear Agreement

The scandal has extended far beyond domestic legal matters, creating severe diplomatic friction between Abu Dhabi and Washington. Most notably, the fallout has directly impacted a landmark civil nuclear cooperation deal—known as a "123 Agreement"—between the United States and the United Arab Emirates.

The agreement, designed to allow the UAE to acquire US nuclear technology and materials for peaceful energy generation, was previously hailed as a "gold standard" for non-proliferation in the Middle East. However, the release of the torture video triggered bipartisan fury on Capitol Hill. Key US lawmakers expressed deep concern over doing business with a regime that appeared to grant impunity to high-ranking royals guilty of egregious human rights violations. 

Congressional leaders called for a halt to the ratification of the nuclear deal until the UAE government could demonstrate a genuine commitment to the rule of law. As a result, the Obama administration was forced to delay the agreement's progress through Congress, transforming a localized business dispute into a major geopolitical stumbling block.

### Conclusion

The Sheikh Issa torture scandal has exposed a stark contradiction between the UAE's aspirations as a modern, globally integrated nation and the lingering realities of autocratic royal privilege. As Sheikh Issa remains under house arrest, the international community continues to watch closely. The outcome of the investigation will not only determine the future of the US-UAE civil nuclear partnership but will also serve as a defining moment for the credibility of the UAE’s legal system on the world stage.

**Title:** Shadow over the Sands: The 2009 Abu Dhabi Torture Tape Scandal

In April 2009, an investigative report broadcast by ABC News ignited an international firestorm, shattering the carefully cultivated image of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) as a modern, progressive, and law-abiding Gulf nation. At the center of the scandal was a graphic 45-minute video depicting a member of the Abu Dhabi royal family brutally torturing a business associate in the desert. 

The perpetrator was Sheikh Issa bin Zayed Al Nahyan—a son of the UAE’s founder, Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan, and a brother to both the country's then-President, Sheikh Khalifa, and its current President, Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed (MBZ). The incident, which came to be known as the Abu Dhabi torture tape scandal, exposed deep fissures regarding human rights, royal impunity, and diplomatic pragmatism in the Middle East.

---

### The Tape and the Torture

The video footage, filmed around 2004, documented the systematic torture of Silak Abdulkadir, an Afghan grain merchant. The dispute reportedly stemmed from a minor financial disagreement, with Sheikh Issa accusing Abdulkadir of cheating him on a grain delivery worth roughly $5,000.

What made the tape particularly shocking was not only the extreme violence depicted, but the casual involvement of local law enforcement officers. Over forty-five minutes, the video showed Sheikh Issa:
* Beating Abdulkadir with wooden planks spiked with nails.
* Pouring salt into the victim's open wounds.
* Setting fire to the victim’s testicles using lighter fluid.
* Shocking him repeatedly with cattle prods.
* Driving a Mercedes SUV over the victim repeatedly as he lay incapacitated in the desert sand.

Throughout the ordeal, men dressed in UAE police uniforms held the victim down, assisted with the torture equipment, and at one point, tied Abdulkadir’s arms and legs. The video was filmed by a security guard at Sheikh Issa’s explicit request, as the royal allegedly enjoyed reviewing recordings of his violent acts.

---

### How the Footage Emerged

The tape was smuggled out of the UAE by Bassam Nabulsi, a US citizen and former business partner of Sheikh Issa. According to Nabulsi, he had worked closely with the Sheikh for years until their relationship deteriorated when Nabulsi refused to help smuggle drugs and continue filming acts of violence. 

Nabulsi claimed that after refusing to cooperate, he himself was arrested, beaten, and tortured by UAE authorities before being released. Recognizing the danger to his life, Nabulsi fled the country, successfully smuggling out several torture tapes. He later filed a lawsuit in a US federal court against Sheikh Issa and provided the video evidence to ABC News investigative reporter Brian Ross, who broke the story internationally in April 2009.

---

### International Backlash and Diplomatic Fallout

The public release of the footage caused immediate diplomatic humiliation for the UAE and placed its Western allies, particularly the United States, in an uncomfortable position. 

Human rights organizations, including Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International, issued blistering condemnations, demanding a full, independent investigation and accusing the UAE government of harboring a culture of royal impunity. 

In Washington, the scandal threatened a landmark deal: the US-UAE 123 Civil Nuclear Agreement, which would allow the UAE to acquire US nuclear technology and materials. Members of the US Congress, led by lawmakers such as Representative Howard Berman, expressed deep concern, demanding that the Obama administration pause the agreement until the UAE held Sheikh Issa accountable. The US State Department publicly called on the UAE government to fully investigate the allegations.

---

### The Official Response and the "Drugging" Defense

Initially, the UAE Interior Ministry—headed by another brother of Sheikh Issa, Sheikh Saif bin Zayed—issued a statement claiming the matter had been "reviewed and resolved privately" between the involved parties, asserting that standard procedures had been followed. 

However, as international pressure intensified and the nuclear deal hung in the balance, the UAE government altered its stance. Abu Dhabi authorities announced that Sheikh Issa had been placed under house arrest and would face trial—an unprecedented move against a member of the ruling family.

The trial took place in the Emirate of Al Ain between late 2009 and early 2010. Sheikh Issa’s defense team argued that the Sheikh was not responsible for his actions because he was the victim of a conspiracy. They claimed that Bassam Nabulsi and his brother had secretly administered a cocktail of mind-altering drugs to the Sheikh—including medication that induced severe aggression and loss of self-control—specifically to orchestrate and record the acts to blackmail him.

---

### The Verdict and Aftermath

In January 2010, the court delivered its verdict: Sheikh Issa was fully acquitted of all charges on the grounds of "diminished responsibility" due to the alleged drugging. 

Conversely, the court sentenced the victim's supporters and the whistleblowers. Bassam Nabulsi and his brother were tried in absentia and sentenced to five years in prison for libel, blackmail, and illegal video recording. Several lower-level police officers involved in the video received relatively light sentences or probation.

Human rights advocacy groups widely condemned the verdict as a whitewash designed to preserve the untouchable status of the UAE royal family while offering just enough process to satisfy foreign governments. 

Despite the controversy, the diplomatic storm eventually cleared. The US-UAE Nuclear Agreement was subsequently ratified, as Washington prioritized strategic, economic, and security ties with Abu Dhabi over human rights enforcement in this case.

---

### Legacy of the Scandal

The 2009 torture tape scandal remains a pivotal case study in the dynamics of rule of law within absolute monarchies. It highlighted the stark contrast between the UAE’s modern, luxurious exterior and the legal immunity enjoyed by its ruling elite behind closed doors. 

While the incident forced the UAE to modernize its public relations and crisis management capabilities, the ultimate acquittal of Sheikh Issa solidified the perception that, within the political framework of the UAE, true accountability for the highest tiers of royalty remains out of reach.
